title: Low-\(n\) Boolean algebra conjecture
formal: For every finite \(n\ge1\), does every countable Boolean algebra with a low-\(n\) presentation also have a computable presentation, where low-\(n\) means that its atomic diagram has \(n\)-th jump equivalent to \(\emptyset^{(n)}\)?
definitions: Definitions and model details remain incomplete. Specify the presentation language and atomic-diagram coding; verify the exact range of the established small-\(n\) cases.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the stated existence or universal proposition, or of its logical negation. This is a provisional candidate, not a completed benchmark specification. Pending: Specify the presentation language and atomic-diagram coding; verify the exact range of the established small-\(n\) cases.

why: This tests whether a weak noncomputable presentation of an algebra can always be replaced by a computable one.

import_provenance.original_statement: For every finite n, does any countable Boolean algebra having a low_n presentation also have a computable presentation? Here low_n means that the n-th Turing jump of its atomic diagram is equivalent to the n-th jump of the computable sets; Knight and Stob established the result through n=4.
